title: Google Maps
problem: Design a web-scale map service that renders tiled maps, searches places, and computes routes from A to B.
summary: A read-heavy geospatial system dominated by three very different workloads: (1) map tile fetches — billions of tiny immutable PNG/vector requests that belong on a CDN, (2) place autocomplete — low-latency prefix search out of Elasticsearch, and (3) routing — CPU-heavy graph traversal over the road network, accelerated with Contraction Hierarchies so 1000 km queries finish in <100ms. The dominant design choice is pushing the tile workload all the way to the CDN edge (99%+ cache hit) so the origin sees only rare misses; the main tradeoff is that map updates take hours to propagate globally as tiles are re-rendered and purged. Sized for ~1B MAU and ~10M route requests/day.

functional: Serve raster or vector map tiles addressed by (z, x, y) for zoom levels 0-22.
Resolve a free-text place query to ranked candidate locations with autocomplete.
Compute driving, walking, cycling, and transit routes between two coordinates.
Return live ETA for an active route, incorporating current traffic.
Let clients request a route alternative or avoid-tolls / avoid-highways variant.
Expose a /places/{id} endpoint for the place details card.
nonFunctional: Tile cache hit ratio above 99 percent at the edge; cold tiles under 300 ms p99.
Route computation p99 under 500 ms for intra-country trips.
Autocomplete p99 under 80 ms per keystroke.
Tile storage is immutable and versioned so rolling back a bad render is instant.
99.99 percent regional availability; degraded mode returns stale traffic rather than error.
Horizontally scalable to 1B+ DAU with regional graph partitioning.

assumptions: Average user loads ~100 map tiles per session (viewport + pan)
Tile pyramid: zoom 0 to 21, ~5T unique tiles at z=21 (mostly ocean/empty → not stored)
Vector tiles (mvt) ≈ 20 KB each after compression; raster PNG ≈ 100 KB
estimates: Tile QPS: 200M * 100 / 86400 ≈ 230K tile fetches/sec → >99% CDN hit → origin ≈ 2K QPS
Place search QPS: 50M / 86400 ≈ 580 QPS, peak ~2K QPS
Tile storage: ~200 TB of vector tiles (world coverage, z=0..17) + incremental updates
Road graph: ~2B nodes / 3B edges worldwide; fits in ~80 GB RAM per routing server after CH preprocessing

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> cdn[CDN Edge] cdn --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> api[Maps API] api --> tiles[Tile Service] api --> geocode[Geocoding Service] api --> route[Routing Service] api --> place[Place Search] tiles --> tcache[(Tile Cache)] tiles --> tblob[(Tile Blob Store)]

client.name: Client (Browser / Mobile SDK)
client.summary: Map canvas that computes the visible tile set and fetches z/x/y tiles, plus UI for search and routing.

sections.heading: Tile math
sections.body: Given viewport center (lat, lng) and zoom z, client computes `x = floor((lng+180)/360 * 2^z)` and `y = floor((1 - ln(tan(lat)+sec(lat))/π)/2 * 2^z)`. Web Mercator projection (EPSG:3857). Requests ~9 tiles for a single desktop viewport + 1-tile ring prefetch = ~25 tiles.

sections.heading: Caching
sections.body: Browser HTTP cache + IndexedDB for offline. Mobile SDKs also cache vector tiles for the last N downloaded regions.

sections.heading: Why this matters
sections.body: A typical pan triggers 5-10 new tile GETs. At 200ms visible-delay budget, each tile must arrive in <50ms — which is only feasible from an edge POP, not the origin.

bottlenecks.title: Tile fetch burst per pan exceeds browser connection budget
bottlenecks.trigger: A single pan dispatches ~9 viewport tiles + 1-ring prefetch ≈ 25 tile GETs within ~10ms; on HTTP/1.1 fallback the browser caps at 6 connections per origin, queueing 19 requests.
bottlenecks.symptom: Visible tile pop-in and grey squares during pans; p95 viewport paint blows past the 200ms budget even though each tile arrives in <50ms from the CDN.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) end-to-end so all 25 tiles multiplex on one connection; shard tile hostnames (tile0/1/2.maps...) as an HTTP/1.1 fallback; cap prefetch ring to 1 and cancel in-flight tiles when the viewport changes (AbortController).
bottlenecks.detection: RUM metric `tileRequestQueueTime` (time between fetch call and actual network send) — alert when p95 > 20ms, which indicates the browser is queueing behind the 6-connection limit.

bottlenecks.title: IndexedDB tile cache bloat and eviction storms
bottlenecks.trigger: Mobile users caching vector tiles for multiple offline regions; at ~20KB/tile and 100 tiles/session plus offline regions, a heavy user can exceed the browser's per-origin storage quota (typically 50MB–20% of disk) within days.
bottlenecks.symptom: QuotaExceededError on IndexedDB writes; tiles silently stop caching; cold-start map load jumps from <500ms to 2–3s as every tile re-fetches from network.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement LRU eviction keyed by last-access timestamp with a hard cap (e.g. 200MB on mobile, 50MB on web); evict whole zoom levels first (drop z≥15 before z≤10 since low zooms are hotter); expose `navigator.storage.estimate` checks before writes.
bottlenecks.detection: Client telemetry on `QuotaExceededError` rate and `storage.estimate.usage / quota` ratio; alert when >5% of sessions hit >80% quota.

bottlenecks.title: Main-thread jank from vector tile decode + WebGL styling
bottlenecks.trigger: Each pan decodes 9 MVT protobufs (~20KB each, thousands of features) and re-styles them against the active theme on the main thread; at 60fps the budget is 16ms per frame but MVT parse alone can take 20–50ms per tile on mid-range mobile.
bottlenecks.symptom: Scroll/pan stutter, dropped frames, unresponsive UI during map interaction despite tiles arriving quickly over the network.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Move VectorTile.parse + feature styling into a Web Worker (or OffscreenCanvas for WebGL); batch draw calls per style layer rather than per feature; use transferable ArrayBuffers to avoid copy overhead when handing bytes to the worker.
bottlenecks.detection: Long Task API (`PerformanceObserver` for entries >50ms) attributed to tile decode; alert when p95 of `tileDecodeDuration` exceeds 30ms on the 75th-percentile device class.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is a real component here In most system designs the client is a thin shell that just renders whatever the server sends. For Google Maps, that's not true — the client is doing *real work* that the backend fundamentally cannot do. The server has no idea what pixels are on your screen, so it can't know which tiles to send you. The client computes the visible tile set itself using Web Mercator math (`x = floor((lng+180)/360 * 2^z)`), then fetches exactly those 9-ish tiles. It also decodes vector tile protobufs, applies the current style theme, and draws everything to WebGL. Without this, the origin would have to render per-user custom images — impossible at this scale. ## What happens without a smart client If the client were dumb and asked the server "give me a picture of San Francisco at zoom 14," every pan would hit the origin with a unique, uncacheable request. Tile caching collapses. The user sees grey squares for 500ms+ on every drag; the operator sees origin CPU spiking on Mapnik renders; the CDN's 99%+ hit rate evaporates because no two requests share a URL. ## The arithmetic Capacity says 200M DAU × 100 tiles/session ≈ **230K tile fetches/sec**. Because the client reduces each viewport to a deterministic set of `/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt` URLs, those 230K requests collapse onto a tiny shared keyspace — z≤10 is only ~1.4M unique tiles globally — which is why the CDN can cache them with >99% hit rate and the origin only sees ~2K QPS. ## The trade-off Pushing tile math, decoding, and styling to the client means every device needs a non-trivial rendering engine (hence the heavy WebGL + Web Worker work) instead of a simple `` tag.

cdn.name: CDN Edge (Tile POP)
cdn.summary: Global edge network (CloudFront / Fastly / Google's own) caching immutable tile blobs keyed by z/x/y.

sections.heading: Cache key
sections.body: Key = `/tiles/{style}/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt`. Tiles are content-addressed and immutable for 7-30 days; updates roll out with a version prefix (`/tiles/v42/...`) so a global purge is unnecessary.

sections.heading: Hit rate
sections.body: Top of the pyramid (z ≤ 10) is tiny — ~1.4M tiles total — and gets re-requested constantly. Entire subtree stays hot in edge RAM. Combined hit rate across zoom levels routinely exceeds 99%.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Edge miss → origin fetch adds ~50-200ms depending on region.
- Stampede on a newly-released region: request coalescing (single-flight) at the edge saves the origin.

lost: Less tuning of cache eviction vs bespoke CDN

bottlenecks.title: Origin miss stampede on new tile version rollout
bottlenecks.trigger: Publishing a new tile version prefix (e.g. /tiles/v43/...) invalidates the entire ~1.4M hot-tile working set at z≤10; at 230K tile QPS globally, the CDN hit rate collapses from >99% to near 0% for minutes, pushing up to ~230K QPS at the origin vs the ~2K QPS it's sized for (100x overshoot).
bottlenecks.symptom: Origin Tile Service saturates, p95 tile latency jumps from ~20ms to hundreds of ms, users see grey tiles during pans, Tile Blob Store egress spikes and bills balloon.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Stage version cutover: pre-warm edges by crawling the top-N hot tiles (z=0..10 ≈ 1.4M tiles) against the new prefix before flipping clients; enable request coalescing / single-flight at the edge (Fastly shielding, CloudFront Origin Shield, or Cloudflare Tiered Cache) so each POP issues at most one origin fetch per key; ramp traffic to v43 over 30+ minutes with a client-side version flag.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `origin_request_rate` > 10K QPS (5x normal) or `edge_hit_ratio` < 95% over a 1-minute window; dashboard on per-version hit-ratio during the first hour of any rollout.

bottlenecks.title: Cold long-tail tiles (z=18..21) evicting from edge RAM
bottlenecks.trigger: Deep-zoom tiles for non-urban areas are viewed rarely; with ~500 TB total tile corpus and typical POP cache sizes of 1–10 TB, these tiles are evicted between requests. A user exploring at z=20 triggers consistent edge misses for their viewport's 9 tiles.
bottlenecks.symptom: p95 tile latency for zoomed-in views is 50–200ms (origin fetch) instead of <30ms; noticeable tile pop-in on mobile in rural/suburban areas; uneven UX where dense cities feel snappy but edges feel slow.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Introduce a mid-tier regional shield cache (Origin Shield / Tiered Cache) with 50–100 TB capacity per region so POP misses hit warm regional storage in ~10ms instead of walking to S3 at ~30–80ms; tune edge TTLs to 30 days for z≥15 since they change rarely; consider pushing only z≤14 to edge and serving z≥15 from regional tier.
bottlenecks.detection: Segment `edge_hit_ratio` by zoom level; alert when hit ratio for z≥15 drops below 90%, or when `origin_fetch_latency_p95` for high-zoom tiles exceeds 60ms.

bottlenecks.title: Style/locale cache-key explosion fragmenting the hot set
bottlenecks.trigger: Cache key includes `{style}` (e.g. default, dark, satellite, transit) and often Accept-Language headers via Vary; with 4+ styles × 20+ languages, the ~1.4M hot top-of-pyramid tiles fan out to 100M+ unique cache entries, most of which are cold.
bottlenecks.symptom: Reported edge hit rate drifts below the 99% target (e.g. 95–97%), origin QPS creeps from 2K toward 10K+, per-region Redis tile cache sees more fill traffic than expected.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep language out of the tile key — vector tiles ship raw feature names and client applies locale at render time (already true for MVT); limit Vary headers to essentials (accept-encoding only); if style variants share geometry, split into a geometry layer (shared) + style sprite (tiny, separate URL) to collapse the keyspace.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `cache_key_cardinality` per tile path prefix; alert on unexpected growth (>2x week-over-week); monitor `hit_ratio` per style dimension to spot a style variant with anomalously poor caching.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the CDN is here for Google Maps The tile workload is the dominant traffic in this system, and it has a magical property: every user looking at downtown San Francisco at zoom 14 asks for the *exact same bytes* at URL `/tiles/vector/14/2620/6333.mvt`. Tiles are immutable, identical across users, and tiny. That's a textbook case for pushing storage out to edge POPs near the user rather than serving from a central origin. The CDN isn't a nice-to-have here — it's the architectural decision that makes the entire service economically feasible. ## What happens without it Without the CDN, every tile GET walks all the way to a regional origin. A user in Tokyo panning around Shibuya waits ~150ms per tile instead of ~20ms, so pans feel laggy and tiles pop in visibly. The operator sees the Tile Service, Tile Cache (Redis), and Tile Blob Store all getting hammered; origin bandwidth bills explode; and during peak hours the backends simply can't keep up and start shedding load, producing grey squares on maps worldwide. ## The arithmetic Capacity estimates say **230K tile fetches/sec** globally. With a 99%+ edge hit rate, the origin sees 230K × 0.01 ≈ **2.3K QPS** — something a modest fleet can handle. Without the CDN, the origin would need to serve the full 230K QPS, a **100× increase**. Storing hot low-zoom tiles (z≤10 is only ~1.4M tiles) fits trivially in edge RAM, which is why the hit rate is so high. ## The trade-off Because edges cache aggressively, map updates take hours to propagate globally — fixed by versioned URL prefixes (`/tiles/v42/...`) instead of purges.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS LB at each region; routes /tiles/*, /place/*, /route/* to the right backend.

sections.heading: Path-based routing
sections.body: `/tiles/*` → Maps API (which forwards to Tile Service). `/route` → Maps API → Routing. `/place/search` → Maps API → Place Search. Keeping one API tier simplifies auth/rate-limit.

sections.heading: TLS termination
sections.body: Terminates HTTPS at the LB; HTTP/2 inside the VPC. Tile responses benefit strongly from HTTP/2 multiplexing (25 parallel tile fetches on one connection).

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU saturation under tile QPS fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: At 230K tile fetches/sec globally, even with 99%+ CDN hit the ~2K QPS origin miss plus 580 QPS place search, 115 QPS route, and health/auxiliary traffic all terminate TLS at the regional LB. A single L7 LB node handles ~20-40K TLS handshakes/sec before CPU saturates; a CDN version-prefix rollout (e.g. /tiles/v43/...) can stampede the origin to 100K+ QPS, with most being new HTTP/2 connections from edge POPs.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegged at 100%, p99 connection-establishment time jumps from <5ms to 200ms+, new TLS handshakes fail or time out, downstream Maps API sees an artificial traffic drop while clients see 502s and stalled tile loads mid-pan.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS session resumption (session tickets + 24h session cache) to cut full handshakes by >80%; offload to hardware crypto (AWS Network Load Balancer with ALB, or ECDSA certs which are ~4x faster than RSA-2048); horizontally scale LB pool with ECMP/anycast so any single node handles <50% of regional TLS load; enforce HTTP/2 from CDN shield to reuse connections across many tile requests.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU > 70% sustained over 1 min, or `tls_handshake_duration_p99` > 50ms, or `new_connections_per_sec` per node > 70% of measured ceiling; track `tls_session_resumption_ratio` and alert if it drops below 80%.

bottlenecks.title: HTTP/2 stream multiplexing exhaustion from viewport tile bursts
bottlenecks.trigger: Each client pan dispatches ~25 tile GETs multiplexed on a single HTTP/2 connection (per the client design). Default `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` is often 100-250; with 200M DAU and connection coalescing across tabs, a single LB node servicing ~50K concurrent HTTP/2 connections can hit per-connection stream limits, and the LB's global stream table (millions of in-flight streams) consumes memory and scheduling cycles.
bottlenecks.symptom: Clients observe `REFUSED_STREAM` errors requiring retry (visible tile pop-in on fast pans), LB memory grows unexpectedly, p95 `tileRequestQueueTime` on the client climbs above the 20ms alert threshold even though the network is healthy.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` to 512 on the LB (nginx `http2_max_concurrent_streams`, Envoy `max_concurrent_streams`); tune `initial_stream_window_size` to 1MB to avoid flow-control stalls on 20KB MVT payloads; cap per-connection requests and rotate connections every N minutes to bound state; ensure the path `/tiles/*` uses HTTP/2 end-to-end from LB to Tile Service to preserve multiplexing benefits.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `http2_refused_streams_total` and `http2_streams_active` per LB node; alert when refused_streams > 0.01% of total streams or when any node's active streams exceed 80% of the configured max * connection count.

bottlenecks.title: Long-tail routing requests blocking LB connection slots
bottlenecks.trigger: Routing requests take 50-300ms (p99 higher under traffic-layer reloads or 1000km queries), vs <20ms for tiles and <50ms for place search. With peak 500 route QPS and per-connection keep-alive, route calls occupy LB upstream connection slots 10-30x longer than tile calls; a Routing Service graph-reload stall (10min per node during daily deploy) can back up 100K+ in-flight routes on the LB.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB upstream connection pool to Routing saturates, `/route` requests queue on the LB and return 504 Gateway Timeout, `/tiles` and `/place` remain healthy creating confusing partial-outage signals, on-call sees queue-depth alerts on only the routing upstream.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Isolate upstream pools per backend (separate connection pools for Tile/Route/Place/Geocode in Envoy/nginx) so route latency cannot starve tile slots; set per-route circuit breakers (`max_pending_requests`, `max_requests` in Envoy) at ~2x steady-state to fail fast; enforce a 2s hard timeout on `/route` at the LB with retry disabled; use outlier detection to eject stalled Routing pods during graph reloads.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-upstream `upstream_rq_pending_active` and `upstream_cx_active` metrics; alert when pending_active for routing > 100 for >30s, or when `/route` p99 latency at the LB exceeds 500ms while other paths remain normal.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Load Balancer sits here For Google Maps, the traffic arriving at each region is a weird mix: most of it is tile fetches on CDN misses (fast, uniform), but sprinkled in are 580 QPS of place searches and 115 QPS of routing calls that can each take 100-300ms. These workloads hit completely different backends (Tile Service, Elasticsearch, Routing Service) with completely different scaling profiles. The LB is what lets a single public hostname (`maps.googleapis.com`) fan out to the right backend pool based on URL path — `/tiles/*` goes one way, `/route` another — while also terminating TLS once so the backends can speak plain HTTP/2 inside the VPC. ## What happens without it If clients talked directly to backend pods, every deploy or pod restart would break in-flight connections, and there'd be no single place to enforce TLS, rate-limit abusive keys, or drain a bad node. Worse, a slow `/route` call (300ms graph traversal) could occupy a connection slot that a 20ms tile request needed — one backend's latency would poison the others. Operators would see cascading 504s with no clean way to isolate the cause. ## The arithmetic Peak combined origin traffic is ~2K tile QPS + 2K place QPS + 500 route QPS ≈ **4.5K QPS per region**, all multiplexed over HTTP/2. A single LB node handles ~20-40K TLS handshakes/sec, so a small pool (say 4 nodes) covers peak plus a 5× version-rollout stampede comfortably — exactly why the design treats the LB as a thin, stateless tier rather than a scaling concern. ## Trade-off One extra network hop (~1ms) in exchange for clean service isolation and a single control point for auth, TLS, and traffic shaping.

api.name: Maps API Gateway
api.summary: Thin stateless gateway handling auth, quota, and dispatch to Tile/Route/Geocode/Place services.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
GET /tiles/{style}/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt → Tile Service
GET /place/autocomplete?q=... → Place Search
GET /geocode?addr=... → Geocoding
GET /route?origin=..&dest=.. → Routing
```

sections.heading: Auth / quota
sections.body: API key in header or signed URL for mobile. Per-key token bucket enforced via Redis. Free tier is 25k map loads/month per key.

sections.heading: Why a thin gateway
sections.body: Each underlying service has wildly different latency (1ms tile lookup vs 100ms route). Decoupling them into separate pods lets each scale on its own bottleneck (CPU for routing, RAM for Elasticsearch).

bottlenecks.title: Redis token-bucket quota check becomes per-request chokepoint
bottlenecks.trigger: Every request through the gateway (peak ~4.5K QPS per region: 2K tile origin-miss + 2K place search + 500 route) performs a Redis INCR/EXPIRE for per-API-key quota. A single Redis primary handles ~100K ops/sec, but a hot enterprise API key concentrated on one shard (by key hash) can push a single slot to 50K+ ops/sec during tile-miss stampedes (e.g. CDN version cutover driving origin to 100K+ QPS).
bottlenecks.symptom: Gateway p99 latency jumps from ~10ms to 50-200ms as Redis calls queue; sporadic 429s for legitimate traffic when the bucket script times out and fails closed; on-call sees Redis CPU pegged on one shard while others idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a Lua script for atomic check-and-decrement (one RTT instead of two); shard quota keys by `{api_key}:{minute_bucket}` to spread hot keys across slots; add a local in-process token bucket (e.g. 1-second pre-allocation) that only syncs to Redis every N requests; fail-open on Redis timeout with a circuit breaker so quota enforcement degrades gracefully under Redis stress.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `redis_quota_call_duration_p99` > 5ms or `redis_cluster_slot_ops_per_sec` imbalance ratio > 3x across shards; track `quota_check_timeout_rate` and page if > 0.1% over 1 min.

bottlenecks.title: Head-of-line blocking from slow /route calls starving tile/place threads
bottlenecks.trigger: Gateway concurrency cap is 5000. Route calls take 50-300ms (p99 up to 500ms+ during traffic-layer reloads) vs 3-15ms for tile/place dispatch — routes consume 20-30x more thread-time per request. At peak 500 route QPS × 300ms = 150 concurrent route slots; a Routing Service partial outage pushing routes to 2s doubles that to 1000 slots, leaving the gateway saturated for the 2K tile-miss + 2K place QPS it also serves.
bottlenecks.symptom: Tile and place latency inexplicably climb even though Tile Service and Elasticsearch are healthy; on-call sees uniform latency increase across /tiles, /place, /route while only Routing is degraded; eventual 503s as the gateway rejects on concurrency cap.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Isolate per-backend thread/connection pools (bulkheads) — separate gRPC channels and executor pools for Tile/Route/Place/Geocode so one can't exhaust the others; set aggressive per-endpoint timeouts (tile: 200ms, place: 500ms, route: 2s) with no retry on /route; add a circuit breaker on the Routing upstream that sheds load to 503 after consecutive failures rather than queuing.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-endpoint `inflight_requests` gauge; alert when `/route` inflight > 300 for >30s or when p95 latency for /tiles or /place rises while the respective backend's own p95 stays flat (indicates gateway-side queueing).

bottlenecks.title: API key auth cache miss storm on deploy or key-rotation
bottlenecks.trigger: Gateway fronts ~4.5K QPS/region and validates API keys on every request against an in-process LRU cache backed by a key-metadata store. On pod restart (rolling deploy across dozens of pods) or mass cache invalidation (e.g. key revocation event broadcast), all validation traffic misses and stampedes the key-metadata backend at up to 4.5K QPS per newly-started pod.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rolling deploys produce a 30-60s latency spike where gateway p95 jumps from ~10ms to 100ms+; key-metadata DB CPU spikes; rare 502s if key lookups time out and the gateway fails closed on auth.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm the auth cache at pod startup by loading the top-N active API keys (e.g. top 10K by QPS over the last hour) before accepting traffic; use singleflight/request-coalescing on cache misses so concurrent requests for the same unknown key result in one backend fetch; set cache TTL to 5 min with stale-while-revalidate so expiry doesn't cause simultaneous misses; use bounded negative-cache for invalid keys to prevent attack amplification.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `auth_cache_hit_ratio` per pod — alert if it drops below 95% for >1 min post-deploy; monitor `key_metadata_lookup_qps` and page if it exceeds 10x steady-state baseline.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a thin API gateway sits here For Google Maps, three completely different workloads arrive at the same public hostname: tile fetches (~2K origin QPS, each ~10ms), place autocomplete (~2K QPS, ~30ms against Elasticsearch), and routing (~500 QPS, 50-300ms of CPU-heavy graph search). They share exactly two concerns — *is this API key valid?* and *is this caller under their quota?* — and nothing else. The gateway exists to do those two things once, then dispatch each request to a backend that's tuned for its specific bottleneck (CPU for routing, RAM for Elasticsearch, cache hit rate for tiles). Without this split, auth and quota logic get copy-pasted into every backend and drift out of sync. ## What happens without it If clients talked directly to the Tile Service, Routing Service, and Place Search, each team would reimplement API-key validation and the Redis token-bucket quota. A free-tier user hammering the route endpoint would burn through their quota on *that* service while still getting free tile loads — because nobody's coordinating the budget. Operators would see inconsistent 429 behavior across endpoints, and rolling out a new auth scheme (say, signed URLs for mobile) would require a simultaneous deploy of four services. ## The arithmetic Peak combined origin traffic is ~2K tile + 2K place + 500 route ≈ **4.5K QPS per region**. The free tier is 25K map loads/month/key; at ~100 tiles/session that's ~250 sessions/month. Enforcing that cleanly requires one central counter per key — exactly what the gateway's Redis token bucket does, hit once at 4.5K QPS instead of fragmented across four backends. ## The trade-off One extra ~5ms hop on every request, in exchange for keeping each backend focused on its one hard problem.

tiles.name: Tile Service
tiles.summary: Returns vector or raster tiles for a given z/x/y; hits a fast in-region cache first, then blob storage on miss.

sections.heading: Request path
sections.body:
1. Lookup Redis with key `t:{style}:{z}:{x}:{y}:v{version}` — hit returns in <3ms.
2. Miss → read from blob store (~30ms) and backfill cache.
3. Ultra-rare: tile not pre-rendered → dispatch to tile-renderer offline job and return a lower-zoom fallback.

sections.heading: Why pre-rendered, not on-demand
sections.body: Rendering a vector tile from raw OSM data is ~200-500ms. Doing that online at 230K QPS is impossible. Pre-rendering z=0..17 globally and only z=18..21 for populated areas is a classic space/time trade.

sections.heading: Tile formats
sections.body:
- MVT (Mapbox Vector Tile, protobuf) — client styles on the fly, ~20KB/tile.
- PNG raster — simpler clients but 5-10x larger. Google uses both depending on surface (Maps web app = vector, static map API = raster).

gained: Tiles reflect DB state in real time

bottlenecks.title: Redis cache stampede on CDN version cutover
bottlenecks.trigger: When a new tile version prefix (e.g. /tiles/v43/...) is published, the CDN's 99%+ hit rate on the ~1.4M hot z≤10 working set collapses to ~0%. Origin tile QPS spikes from the steady-state ~2K to potentially ~230K (100x), all hitting the regional Tile Cache simultaneously on the first minute of rollout.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis CPU pegs at 100%, p95 tile-service latency jumps from ~5ms to 50-200ms as lookups queue, then concurrency cap of 3000 saturates and the service returns 503s; users see widespread grey tiles during pans; Tile Blob Store egress explodes as misses cascade through.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm Redis by crawling the top-N hot tiles against the new version prefix before flipping clients; implement single-flight/request-coalescing in the Tile Service so concurrent misses on the same key issue one blob fetch (e.g. golang/x/sync singleflight or an in-process waitgroup keyed by tile URL); stage the version rollout over 30+ minutes via a client-side feature flag rather than atomic cutover.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `tile_cache_miss_rate` > 5% over 1 min (vs <1% baseline) or `tile_service_p95_latency_ms` > 50ms; dashboard on per-version hit ratio during the first hour of any deploy; page if `tile_service_inflight_requests` > 2000 (66% of concurrency cap).

bottlenecks.title: Missing-tile fallback path overwhelms offline render queue
bottlenecks.trigger: A user explores an unpopulated region at z=18-21 where tiles were never pre-rendered (only populated areas have z≥18 coverage). Each missing tile dispatches to an offline tile-renderer job costing 200-500ms of Mapnik CPU. A single user panning through rural z=20 can queue 25+ render jobs/pan; a bot or crawler probing deep-zoom coordinates can submit thousands/sec.
bottlenecks.symptom: Tile renderer worker queue depth grows unboundedly, render job latency balloons from seconds to minutes, the Tile Service returns lower-zoom fallbacks (visible blurriness) for legitimate users in adjacent areas waiting on the same workers; cloud compute bill for the render fleet spikes.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Negative-cache missing tiles in Redis with a short TTL (e.g. 1 hour) keyed by `miss:{z}:{x}:{y}` so repeated requests return the fallback without re-queueing; rate-limit render dispatch per API key (e.g. 10/min) and per geographic region; deterministically return the z-2 parent tile upscaled for any z≥18 request outside a whitelisted populated-areas bitmap, skipping the render queue entirely for known-empty regions.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `render_queue_depth` and `render_dispatch_rate` per region; alert if queue depth > 1000 or dispatch rate > 100/sec (10x normal); monitor `tile_miss_to_render_ratio` and alert if >0.1% of misses trigger renders (baseline should be near 0 given pre-render coverage).

bottlenecks.title: Blob store latency spikes dominate p99 under sustained miss load
bottlenecks.trigger: Normal operation has ~2K origin QPS with most served from Redis in ~2ms, but deep-zoom (z≥15) tiles are cold in Redis due to LRU eviction under the ~500GB regional budget vs ~500TB corpus. These miss through to S3/GCS at 10-80ms per fetch. At sustained 200+ QPS of cold-tile traffic (a power user exploring satellite view, or a scraping client), p99 tile-service latency is bounded by blob-store tail latency (80ms) not cache hits.
bottlenecks.symptom: Tile Service p99 latency sits at 80-100ms vs p50 of 5ms; users at zoomed-in views report visible tile pop-in; blob-store bill grows disproportionately to traffic; CDN origin-fetch latency histograms show a bimodal distribution (cache-hit fast path vs blob-miss slow path).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add range-request coalescing and connection pooling to the blob client (e.g. 500 persistent HTTP/2 connections to S3 per tile pod); bias Redis eviction to keep z=0-14 resident by using LFU instead of LRU or by sharding the cache into per-zoom pools with dedicated budgets; pre-fetch sibling tiles (same z/x range) on any z≥15 miss since users pan laterally; set a hard 150ms timeout on blob reads and serve a lower-zoom parent tile on timeout.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `blob_fetch_duration_ms` segmented by zoom level — alert on p99 > 100ms sustained; track `tile_service_p99_latency_ms` and page if > 50ms for >5 min; monitor `redis_eviction_rate` per zoom bucket and alert if z≤10 eviction rate > 0 (those should never evict).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Tile Service exists here For Google Maps, the CDN catches 99%+ of tile traffic — but that leftover 1% still has to land somewhere, and that somewhere is the Tile Service. Its job is narrow: given a `/tiles/{style}/{z}/{x}/{y}` URL, return the pre-rendered bytes as fast as possible. It's the component that owns the answer to "where do tile bytes actually live, and how do we serve a CDN miss in single-digit milliseconds instead of re-rendering from raw map data?" Rendering a vector tile from OpenStreetMap data takes 200–500ms of CPU — doing that online at map-browsing scale is simply impossible, so the Tile Service is really a *lookup* service over a pre-rendered corpus, not a rendering service. ## What happens without it If the CDN missed straight through to the blob store (S3/GCS), every miss would cost 30–80ms and there'd be no place to coalesce duplicate concurrent requests for the same tile. During a new tile version rollout, thousands of edge POPs would simultaneously hammer S3 for the same 1.4M hot tiles, the blob egress bill would explode, and users would see grey squares during pans. There'd also be nowhere to handle the rare "this tile was never pre-rendered" case gracefully. ## The arithmetic Capacity says ~230K tile fetches/sec globally, with >99% absorbed by the CDN → origin sees ~2K QPS. The Tile Service hits Redis first (~2ms), falling back to blob storage (~30ms) only on Redis miss. That two-tier cache turns a worst-case 30ms miss into a typical 3ms response — a 10× win on the origin path. ## Trade-off Pre-rendering the entire world (~500TB) costs enormous storage so that *reads* stay cheap.

tcache.name: Tile Cache (Redis)
tcache.summary: Regional Redis cluster caching recently-served tile bytes.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body: Binary tile bytes keyed by `t:{style}:{z}:{x}:{y}:v{n}`. Values are 20-100 KB. Cluster size ~500 GB/region, LRU eviction at 80% watermark.

sections.heading: Why a second cache behind the CDN
sections.body: The CDN catches the 99%+ hit; the 1% miss stampedes into the origin and we don't want that to walk to S3 every time. Redis absorbs the miss stampede in ~2ms instead of ~30ms.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Redis down → everything falls through to blob, p95 jumps from 5ms → 30ms.
- Hot tile stampede: single-flight request coalescing at the Tile Service layer.

bottlenecks.title: Network bandwidth saturation from large tile payloads
bottlenecks.trigger: At a CDN version cutover, origin tile QPS can spike from steady ~2K to ~100K+ as the 1.4M hot z≤10 working set re-fills. With values averaging 20KB (vector) to 100KB (raster), even steady-state 2K QPS × 20KB = 40 MB/s per region is modest, but a 50K QPS miss stampede × 50KB avg = 2.5 GB/s = 20 Gbps — saturating the NIC on any single Redis primary well before CPU or memory become the limit.
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis `instantaneous_output_kbps` hits NIC ceiling, client-side p99 GET latency jumps from ~2ms to 50-200ms as responses queue in the kernel send buffer, Tile Service falls back to blob store for timed-out cache reads, origin blob egress and S3 bill spike even though Redis reports healthy CPU.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard the cluster across more primaries (≥16 shards per region) to distribute bandwidth; co-locate Redis in the same AZ as Tile Service and use 25 Gbps+ ENIs; enable client-side compression with zstd on tile bytes before SET (MVT is already gzipped but re-wrap with zstd saves ~15%); consider moving to a disk-backed cache like Dragonfly or KeyDB with per-core network scaling for tile-sized payloads.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `redis_net_output_bytes_per_sec` > 70% of NIC capacity per node; histogram `tile_cache_get_duration_ms` p99 > 10ms sustained; track `tile_service_blob_fallback_rate` and page if > 5% (indicates cache timeouts, not true misses).

bottlenecks.title: LRU eviction storm evicts hot z≤10 tiles under deep-zoom miss load
bottlenecks.trigger: Cluster budget is ~500 GB/region against a ~500 TB tile corpus — a 1000:1 ratio. When a burst of cold deep-zoom (z≥15) traffic arrives (satellite-view user, scraping client, or a new region becoming popular), each miss writes a fresh 20-100KB tile at the LRU head, displacing the hot z≤10 working set (~1.4M tiles × 20KB ≈ 28 GB — fits, but only if eviction respects access frequency). Under plain LRU, a scan-like workload can evict the permanently-hot top of the pyramid within minutes.
bottlenecks.symptom: Overall cache hit rate drifts from ~99% toward 90%, Tile Service p95 rises from 5ms to 30ms as more requests walk to blob, CDN origin-fetch latency worsens, and subsequent re-fills of the hot set cause secondary bandwidth spikes (see bottleneck #1) in a feedback loop.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Switch eviction policy from `allkeys-lru` to `allkeys-lfu` (configure `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu` with `lfu-log-factor 10`) so rarely-accessed deep-zoom tiles don't displace constantly-hit z≤10 tiles; alternatively shard cache into per-zoom-band pools with dedicated budgets (e.g. z=0-10 gets 40% of RAM, z=11-14 gets 40%, z≥15 gets 20%); pin the top ~2M hottest tiles via a warm-set process that periodically re-TOUCHes them.
bottlenecks.detection: Segment `tile_cache_hit_ratio` by zoom level and alert when z≤10 hit ratio drops below 99.5%; track `redis_evicted_keys` per second and alert on >1000/sec sustained; monitor the ratio `evictions_of_z≤10 / total_evictions` and page if >1% (those tiles should effectively never evict).

bottlenecks.title: Single-key hotspot on viral tiles concentrated on one shard
bottlenecks.trigger: Cache keys are `t:{style}:{z}:{x}:{y}:v{n}` hashed to a single slot, so a viral tile (e.g. downtown Tokyo at z=14 during a live event, or a tile showcased in a news article) concentrates QPS on one primary. At a 99% CDN hit ratio, a tile viewed globally at 10K QPS still lands 100 QPS on the origin — but during an edge-miss event or a POP cold-start, that single tile can hit 2-5K QPS on one Redis shard while 15 other shards sit idle.
bottlenecks.symptom: One Redis primary's CPU pegs at 100% while cluster-aggregate CPU looks healthy (<30%), p99 GET latency for that specific key climbs to 20-50ms, `CLUSTER SLOTS` dashboard shows imbalance, Tile Service threads waiting on that shard starve other tile requests via shared connection pools.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Detect hot keys with `redis-cli --hotkeys` or the Tile Service's own per-key request counter; for detected hot tiles, replicate across N shards with suffixed keys (`t:...:v42:r0`..`r7`) and client-side random-pick on read; add a small in-process L1 LRU (e.g. 10K entries, 200MB per Tile Service pod) for tiles seen >10 times/second, absorbing hotspots before they reach Redis; use Redis replica-reads (`READONLY` mode) to spread GET load across the primary's replicas.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-shard `instantaneous_ops_per_sec` imbalance ratio > 5x across the cluster; `redis_commandstats` per-key tracking (enable `latency-monitor-threshold 10`); alert on any single slot exceeding 30K ops/sec or p99 latency diverging from cluster median by >20ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Redis cache sits behind the CDN For Google Maps, the CDN already absorbs 99%+ of tile traffic at the edge. So why bother with a second cache in the origin region? Because the 1% that *misses* the CDN still stampedes into the origin, and we absolutely do not want each of those requests walking to S3/GCS for a ~30ms blob read. The Tile Cache is the shock absorber between the CDN and the blob store: it keeps the most recently-served tile bytes in RAM so a CDN miss resolves in ~2ms instead of ~30ms, and so a rare but inevitable miss stampede (say, a new tile version rollout that invalidates the global edge cache) doesn't flatten the blob store. ## What happens without it If you removed Redis, a CDN version cutover would collapse the edge hit rate from 99% to near 0% for a few minutes. Every one of those requests now walks straight to S3. The user sees grey tiles during pans; the operator sees S3 egress bills spike and p95 tile latency jump from ~5ms to ~30ms; the Tile Service fleet saturates because each request now holds a thread for 10x longer. ## The arithmetic Origin sees ~2K tile QPS steady-state. A version-cutover stampede can push that to ~100K QPS for a minute. At 30ms per blob fetch, serving 100K QPS would require ~3000 concurrent blob connections; at 2ms per Redis hit, the same load needs only ~200. Redis turns a capacity crisis into a non-event. ## Trade-off You pay ~500GB of RAM per region, and accept that a Redis outage degrades p95 from 5ms to 30ms rather than taking the system down.

tblob.name: Tile Blob Store
tblob.summary: Object storage (S3/GCS) holding all pre-rendered tiles worldwide, versioned.

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body: `s3://maps-tiles-prod/vector/v42/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt` — path acts as the key. Tiles immutable; updates publish a new version prefix.

sections.heading: Size
sections.body: ~200 TB of vector tiles for world coverage z=0..17. Add z=18..21 for cities → ~500 TB. Replicated across 3 regions for multi-region reads.

sections.heading: Why immutable versioning
sections.body: Overwriting a tile would require purging every CDN edge that cached it — costly and slow. Versioned prefixes let us publish atomically and deprecate old versions after 30 days.

bottlenecks.title: CDN version cutover stampede overwhelms blob egress
bottlenecks.trigger: Publishing a new version prefix (e.g. /tiles/v43/...) invalidates the ~1.4M hot z≤10 working set across all CDN edges and the regional Redis cache; origin miss rate jumps from <1% toward 100%, pushing blob QPS from steady-state ~200 (after Redis absorbs most misses) to 50-100K+ concurrent GETs for the same small hot set, each 20-100KB, within the first minute.
bottlenecks.symptom: S3/GCS request rate limits kick in returning 503 SlowDown errors, blob p99 latency climbs from ~30ms to 500ms+, egress bill spikes 10-50x for the day, Tile Service threads stall waiting on blob reads and start returning 503s, users see widespread grey tiles globally.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pre-warm edges and regional Redis against the new version prefix before flipping the client feature flag (crawl top 1.4M z≤10 tiles); enforce request coalescing (singleflight) at the Tile Service so concurrent misses on the same key issue one blob GET; use S3 request-rate-aware prefix sharding (spread /v43/{z}/{x}/{y} across hashed subprefixes); stage rollouts over 30+ minutes rather than atomic cutover.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `s3_5xx_rate` > 0.1% or `s3_slowdown_count` > 0 sustained; track `blob_get_qps` and page when it exceeds 5K (25x baseline); dashboard egress bytes/sec per version prefix during the first hour of any rollout.

bottlenecks.title: Cross-region read latency on multi-region failover or cold deep-zoom
bottlenecks.trigger: Blobs are replicated across 3 regions but a regional outage or an unbalanced Redis eviction for cold z≥15 tiles forces reads from a non-local region; cross-region S3 GET adds 60-150ms vs 10-30ms same-region, and ~500TB corpus means z≥15 tiles are frequently cold in the local edge and Redis.
bottlenecks.symptom: Tile Service p99 latency bimodal — fast local hits at ~30ms plus a slow tail at 100-200ms; user-visible tile pop-in at deep zoom in rural areas; CDN origin-fetch p95 exceeds the 80ms design budget; egress bill shows unexpected cross-region traffic line items.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Pin the Tile Service's blob client to same-region endpoints with S3 Transfer Acceleration or GCS dual-region buckets only as fallback; add a regional shield cache (Origin Shield / Tiered Cache, 50-100TB) in front of blob so POP misses resolve in ~10ms without walking to object storage; set a hard 150ms blob read timeout and return the z-2 parent tile upscaled on timeout.
bottlenecks.detection: Segment `blob_fetch_duration_ms` by source-region vs target-region; alert when cross-region read ratio > 1% or p99 > 100ms sustained; track `blob_timeout_fallback_rate` and page if > 0.5%.

bottlenecks.title: Storage and version-retention bloat from immutable versioned prefixes
bottlenecks.trigger: Each tile-render release publishes a new version prefix (~500TB per version for full z=0..21 coverage including cities); with a 30-day deprecation window and monthly-to-weekly release cadence, 2-5 overlapping versions can coexist, pushing total storage to 1-2.5PB × 3-region replication = 3-7.5PB; partial re-renders (e.g. only changed regions) still produce full new-prefix copies if naïvely implemented.
bottlenecks.symptom: Storage bill grows linearly with release frequency rather than with world coverage; old versions fail to GC because some clients/edges still reference them; compliance/audit queries for 'what did tile X look like on date Y' become expensive; S3 lifecycle rules misfire and either delete live versions or retain dead ones for months.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement content-addressed storage — hash tile bytes and store by digest with version prefixes as symlink-like manifests (only changed tiles allocate new bytes, unchanged tiles dedupe across versions); enforce S3 lifecycle rules transitioning old versions to Glacier Deep Archive after 7 days and deleting after 30; track edge/client references to old versions via access logs and only GC versions with zero traffic for 7+ consecutive days.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `blob_storage_tb_per_version` and `unique_object_count` — alert when version count > 5 or total TB > 2x single-version baseline; monitor `get_qps_per_version` and flag versions with <10 QPS as GC candidates; weekly report on dedup ratio across versions (should be >80% for typical map updates).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a blob store sits at the bottom of the tile stack For Google Maps, every map tile the world has ever seen has to live *somewhere* durable. Rendering a vector tile from raw OpenStreetMap data costs 200–500ms of CPU — far too slow to do on demand at map-browsing scale. So the design pre-renders the entire world offline and parks the output in object storage (S3 / GCS). The Tile Blob Store is that ground-truth corpus: the CDN and Redis are just fast caches in front of it, and on a cache miss *this* is what has the actual bytes. ## What happens without it If there were no durable blob store, the Tile Service would have to re-render tiles from the raw map database on every CDN+Redis miss. A user panning around a lightly-visited region (say, rural Montana at zoom 16) would stare at grey squares for half a second per tile. Operators would see the Mapnik render fleet pegged at 100% CPU during any CDN purge, and a new tile version rollout — which invalidates the edge cache globally — would be effectively impossible because the origin couldn't keep up. ## The arithmetic Capacity says ~500 TB of pre-rendered tiles (z=0..17 worldwide plus z=18..21 for cities). At ~20 KB per vector tile, that's roughly **25 billion tiles** sitting on disk. No database or RAM-based store fits that cheaply — object storage at ~$0.02/GB/month costs ~$10K/month per replica, which is negligible next to the render CPU it saves. ## Trade-off Immutable versioned prefixes (`/v42/...`) mean map updates take hours to propagate globally, in exchange for atomic publishes without CDN purges.

geocode.name: Geocoding Service
geocode.summary: Converts addresses ↔ lat/lng using an in-memory trie of normalised addresses plus fallback to interpolation on road segments.

sections.heading: Forward geocoding
sections.body: `'1600 Amphitheatre Pkwy, Mountain View'` → (37.4225, -122.0844). Tokenise, normalise, then trie lookup followed by re-ranking using postal hierarchy.

sections.heading: Reverse geocoding
sections.body: (37.4225, -122.0844) → nearest address. Uses a spatial index (R-tree) keyed by lng/lat buckets, ordered by street segment.

sections.heading: Why separate from Place Search
sections.body: Geocoding is deterministic (address → point); Place Search is relevance-ranked prefix search. Different indexing strategies and latency profiles.

bottlenecks.title: In-memory address trie RAM bloat and cold-start reload
bottlenecks.trigger: The global normalized-address trie plus R-tree spatial index must fit in RAM on each geocoder pod; at ~1B addresses worldwide with ~100 bytes/entry after normalization, that's ~100GB per pod. A rolling deploy or crash-restart requires reading and reconstructing indexes from snapshot (~10+ min per node) while remaining pods absorb full traffic.
bottlenecks.symptom: During deploys, 1/N of the fleet is unavailable for 10+ min; surviving pods see their share of ~230 QPS avg (peak ~800 QPS derived from the 50M searches/day pattern applied to geocode) double or triple, p99 latency jumps from ~15ms to 50-100ms, and cold pods return 503 until indexes finish loading.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use mmap-backed trie/R-tree files on local NVMe so restart is seconds not minutes (FST-style like Lucene, or RocksDB with bloom filters); pre-warm pods out of the LB pool and only add them once index load + health check passes; shard the index geographically (e.g. by country or S2 cell) so each pod holds ~10-20GB instead of 100GB and reloads proportionally faster.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `geocode_index_load_duration_seconds` > 120s, `geocode_pod_memory_rss_bytes` > 80% of container limit, and `geocode_healthy_pods_ratio` < 0.9 during deploys; track p99 latency divergence between freshly-started and steady-state pods.

bottlenecks.title: Reverse-geocode R-tree hotspot on dense urban lat/lng buckets
bottlenecks.trigger: Reverse geocoding uses an R-tree keyed by lng/lat buckets; in dense urban areas (Manhattan, Tokyo, central London) a single bucket can hold 50-100K street segments. Queries like reverse-geocoding every GPS ping from rideshare/delivery apps concentrate on <1% of buckets holding >50% of addresses, and each lookup walks many overlapping bounding boxes before finding the nearest segment.
bottlenecks.symptom: Bimodal latency distribution — rural reverse-geocode queries return in ~5ms while urban queries take 30-80ms; p99 is dominated by dense-city traffic; CPU profiler shows >60% of time in R-tree node traversal and segment distance calculations.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a multi-level spatial index: coarse S2 cell (level 13, ~1km²) → fine R-tree within cell, so urban cells stay small and uniformly sized; cache recent reverse-geocode results in a small LRU keyed by rounded lat/lng (6 decimals ≈ 10cm) since repeated GPS pings from moving vehicles often land on the same segment; precompute nearest-segment for a grid of sample points in ultra-dense cells.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `reverse_geocode_duration_ms` segmented by S2 cell density class (urban/suburban/rural); alert when urban p99 > 50ms; track `rtree_nodes_visited_per_query` and page if p99 > 500 nodes.

bottlenecks.title: Ambiguous forward-geocode queries fan out to expensive re-ranking
bottlenecks.trigger: Queries like '123 Main St' (with no city) match thousands of candidates globally; trie lookup returns a large candidate set that must be re-ranked by postal hierarchy, user viewport bias, and string similarity. Without a viewport hint or when users paste partial addresses, a single query can evaluate 10K+ candidates at ~10µs each = 100ms of pure CPU.
bottlenecks.symptom: Long-tail latency — p50 ~10ms but p99 climbs past 200ms and occasionally hits the 500ms timeout; CPU-bound pods hit the 3000 concurrency ceiling when ambiguous queries coincide (e.g. batch geocode API users submitting unnormalized CSV addresses); downstream API Gateway sees `/geocode` head-of-line blocking.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap candidate set at top-N (e.g. 200) after trie lookup using pre-indexed importance scores (postal code coverage, address density); require or strongly bias toward a `viewport` or `region` parameter and short-circuit to regional shards; add a per-query CPU budget (e.g. 50ms) and return best-so-far results rather than timing out; cache normalized query → top-K results in Redis with 1h TTL for common ambiguous strings.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `geocode_candidate_set_size` histogram — alert on p99 > 5000; monitor `geocode_cpu_time_ms` per request and page on p99 > 100ms; log queries that exceed budget and feed them to offline analysis for index improvements.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Geocoding sits next to Place Search and Routing For Google Maps, the other services only speak in coordinates. The Routing Service needs a lat/lng to snap onto a road graph node — it has no idea what "1600 Amphitheatre Pkwy" means. The Tile Service draws pixels at a given z/x/y, not at an address. But *users* type addresses, and apps built on the Maps API (Uber, DoorDash, Zillow) send structured address strings by the million. Geocoding is the translation layer: address → lat/lng on the way in, and lat/lng → nearest address on the way out (the "reverse" path rideshare apps use to show "picking you up at 425 Market St"). ## What happens without it If you removed it, every caller would have to bring their own address parser and postal database, which is an enormous amount of locale-specific logic (Japanese addresses don't have street names; UK postcodes mean something very different from US ZIPs). A request for directions from "SF" to "LA" would fail at the Routing Service because it can't snap a string to a graph node. Operators would see routing 4xx rates spike and Place Search getting abused as a geocoder (wrong index, wrong ranking). ## The arithmetic It's kept separate from Place Search because the workloads differ: geocoding is *deterministic* lookup (one right answer per address) while Place Search is *ranked* prefix search over 200M places. Different indexes (trie + R-tree vs Elasticsearch edge-ngrams), different latency budgets (5-20ms vs 10-50ms), different scaling curves — fusing them would compromise both. ## Trade-off Two services to operate instead of one, in exchange for each being tuned to its own access pattern.

place.name: Place Search (Elasticsearch)
place.summary: Prefix-matching autocomplete with geographic boost and popularity scoring, backed by Elasticsearch.

sections.heading: Index
sections.body: One document per place (~200M globally). Fields: name, address, geohash, category, rating, review_count. Custom analyzer handles edge-ngrams for prefix matching and language-specific tokenisation.

sections.heading: Query
sections.body: Edge-ngram match on `name` + geo_distance boost relative to the user's current location + function_score using `log(review_count + 1)` for popularity.

sections.heading: Why Elasticsearch, not DB LIKE
sections.body: Prefix LIKE queries don't use indexes well and can't combine geo proximity + text + popularity in a single ranked pass. Elasticsearch's function_score query is purpose-built for this three-way ranking.

gained: Tiny memory footprint for name-only search
lost: Re-implementing relevance ranking, geo-boost, multilingual yourself

bottlenecks.title: Edge-ngram index RAM bloat across 200M place docs
bottlenecks.trigger: Indexing 200M place documents with edge-ngram analyzer (min_gram=2, max_gram=20) on the `name` field expands the inverted index 10-15x vs standard tokenization; combined with geo_point doc_values, category keywords, and multilingual variants, the index reaches ~2-4 TB. At peak 2K QPS of autocomplete queries each doing function_score with geo_distance + log(review_count), heap pressure on data nodes hitting 30GB+ JVM heap triggers frequent old-gen GC.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 autocomplete latency climbs from ~30ms to 200-500ms during GC pauses; sporadic `circuit_breaking_exception` (fielddata/request breakers tripping); query rejection from the search threadpool under burst load; on-call sees node CPU pegged on GC threads while query CPU is idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Cap edge-ngram max_gram at 10 (most prefixes are short) and use `search_as_you_type` field type instead of full edge-ngram analyzer to cut index size ~3x; shard the index to 20-30 primary shards so each shard heap stays <20GB; switch JVM to G1GC with `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`; move geo_point and review_count to doc_values-only (no fielddata); use dedicated coordinating nodes so query fan-out doesn't compete with data-node heap.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `jvm_gc_old_collection_time_seconds` > 1s/min per node, `indices_query_cache_evictions` spike, or `thread_pool_search_rejected` > 0; dashboard p99 `took` segmented by shard; track heap usage post-GC and page when >75% sustained.

bottlenecks.title: Shard fan-out amplification on prefix-match queries
bottlenecks.trigger: Each autocomplete query (peak 2K QPS) fans out to all primary/replica shards of the places index because edge-ngram prefix matches can live in any shard — there's no natural routing key. With 20+ shards per region, 2K external QPS becomes 40K+ internal shard-level queries; the coordinating node must gather, re-score, and merge top-5 from every shard before responding.
bottlenecks.symptom: Search threadpool queue depth grows on data nodes, `took` latency at coordinator is bounded by the slowest shard (tail amplification — p99 coordinator = p99.95 of shards); a single slow/GC'ing node poisons cluster-wide p99; autocomplete latency spikes during index merges on any single shard.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Route by coarse geohash prefix (e.g. geohash-3 → ~150km cell) so queries hit only 2-4 shards instead of all; use `search_type=dfs_query_then_fetch` only when scoring accuracy demands it; enable adaptive replica selection (`cluster.routing.use_adaptive_replica_selection: true`) so slow replicas are skipped; set `search.default_search_timeout` to 100ms so one slow shard can't drag p99 past the latency budget; pre-filter by region-shard at the API layer using the caller's lat/lng.
bottlenecks.detection: Compare `indices.search.query_time_in_millis` per shard — alert when max/median shard latency ratio > 3x; track `search.fetch_rejected` and `thread_pool.search.queue`; histogram p99 query latency vs number of shards queried per request.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key/viral-place query skew concentrates on few shards
bottlenecks.trigger: Popular prefixes ('star', 'mc', 'pizz') and viral places (new restaurant opening, trending tourist spot) concentrate QPS on the shards holding those docs' term dictionaries; geohash-based sharding worsens this for dense metros (Manhattan, Tokyo) where one shard holds 5-10x the docs of a rural shard. At 2K QPS, a hot prefix like 'star' during a viral event can drive 500+ QPS to a single shard's 1-2 replicas.
bottlenecks.symptom: One data node's CPU pegs at 100% while cluster average is <40%; p99 autocomplete latency for specific prefixes/regions spikes to 200ms+ while others remain <30ms; `_nodes/hot_threads` shows that node stuck in lucene `TermsEnum.seekExact` or function_score loops; uneven replica load visible in Kibana monitoring.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a small in-process LRU cache at the API layer for `(prefix, geohash-5)` → top-5 results with 60s TTL, absorbing repeat queries before they hit ES; increase replica count from 1 to 3 for hot regions and rely on adaptive replica selection for load spreading; split dense-metro geohash cells into sub-shards via custom routing; enable request cache (`indices.requests.cache.enable: true`) for the filter+function_score query shape.
bottlenecks.detection: Track per-shard QPS imbalance ratio (max/mean) — alert when >4x; monitor `indices.request_cache.hit_count` / `miss_count` ratio; log top-N query prefixes per minute and alert on any prefix exceeding 5% of total QPS; per-node CPU stddev > 30% of mean.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Elasticsearch sits here for Google Maps When a user types "pizz" into the Maps search box, they expect three things to happen at once: match anything starting with those letters, prefer places near them over places across the world, and rank popular places (many reviews, high rating) above obscure ones. A regular database `WHERE name LIKE 'pizz%'` can do the first part poorly and the other two not at all — it can't blend text relevance, geographic distance, and popularity into a single ranked result in one pass. Elasticsearch's `function_score` query is purpose-built for exactly this three-way ranking, which is why it owns the autocomplete path separately from Geocoding (which is deterministic address lookup, not ranking). ## What breaks without it If you tried to serve autocomplete from a SQL database, each keystroke would either scan millions of rows or return a naive alphabetical prefix list — "Pizza Hut" on the other side of town beats "Pizzeria Delfina" a block away. Users see irrelevant suggestions and stop trusting search. Operators see database CPU spiking on every keystroke because prefix queries don't use B-tree indexes well, and the Geocoding Service starts getting abused as a fuzzy search engine (wrong index, wrong latency profile). ## The arithmetic Capacity says **50M place searches/day ≈ 580 QPS average, ~2K QPS at peak**, ranking across ~200M place documents globally. At 2K QPS, you have a 10-50ms budget per query to match a prefix, filter by `geo_distance` within 50km, and re-score by `log(review_count)` — Elasticsearch handles this with sharded inverted indexes and geo doc-values; a row-store database cannot. ## Trade-off You run a second stateful system (ES cluster, ~2-4TB index) alongside your primary DB, in exchange for sub-50ms ranked search that a general-purpose database fundamentally can't deliver.

route.name: Routing Service
route.summary: Computes shortest paths on the road graph using Contraction Hierarchies preprocessing for sub-100ms continent-scale queries.

sections.heading: Why not plain Dijkstra
sections.body: Dijkstra on a 2B-node global graph takes seconds per query. Contraction Hierarchies (CH) preprocesses shortcut edges so a bidirectional search visits only ~1000 nodes even for 1000 km queries.

sections.heading: Preprocessing
sections.body: Offline job ranks nodes by importance (centrality) and iteratively contracts least-important nodes, adding shortcut edges that preserve shortest paths. Produces an augmented graph that's ~2-3x the original size but searchable in milliseconds.

sections.heading: Dynamic costs
sections.body: Live traffic modifies edge weights. CH with customisable weights (CCH) lets traffic layer plug in without re-running the full preprocess — critical for rush-hour reroutes.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Graph reload (daily) takes ~10min per node; rolling deploy over the fleet.
- Memory pressure: 80GB graph × 3 replicas/region × N regions. Snapshot on SSD allows fast restart.

bottlenecks.title: 80GB CH graph reload stalls rolling deploys and starves capacity
bottlenecks.trigger: Daily graph reloads take ~10 min per node to load the 80GB CH-augmented graph from snapshot into RAM. With 3 replicas/region and the service sized for peak 500 route QPS at 50-300ms each (~100-150 concurrent slots steady-state), taking one replica out for 10 min shifts load onto the remaining 2 — pushing per-node concurrency from ~50 to ~75 while the service concurrency cap is 500 per pod but CPU-bound well before that.
bottlenecks.symptom: During rolling deploys, /route p99 climbs from ~200ms to 800ms+; LB upstream pool for Routing saturates and returns 504s; on-call sees correlated spikes at deploy boundaries; API Gateway's /route inflight metric pegs while Tile/Place stay flat.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use mmap-backed graph files on local NVMe so reload is I/O-bound seconds instead of 10 min of deserialization; pre-warm pods out of the LB pool and only admit after a synthetic 1000km query returns <150ms; cap concurrent replicas-in-reload at 1 per region via PodDisruptionBudget; keep an N+2 replica count so two simultaneous restarts don't push survivors past 70% CPU.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `routing_graph_load_duration_seconds` > 120s, `routing_healthy_replicas_per_region` < 3, and divergence between p99 of freshly-started vs warm pods > 2x; page when any region's aggregate route CPU exceeds 70% sustained for 2 min.

bottlenecks.title: Long-tail cross-continent queries blow the 500-concurrency budget
bottlenecks.trigger: Service sim models 50-300ms per query with concurrency cap 500. A 1000km query visits ~1284 nodes and finishes <100ms, but pathological inputs (cross-continent trucking routes, queries near disconnected islands, dense urban meshes like Tokyo at rush hour with live traffic reweighting) can visit 100K+ nodes and take 1-2s. At peak 500 QPS × 1s worst case = 500 concurrent slots — the exact cap — so even a 1% tail of slow queries (5 QPS × 2s = 10 slots) on top of 500ms p95 traffic saturates the pod.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-pod concurrency gauge hits 500, new route requests return 503 from the service or 504 from the LB; p99 latency flatlines at the 2s timeout while p50 stays healthy at 80ms; CPU profiler shows a handful of threads stuck in `unpack_shortcuts` or bidirectional Dijkstra heap ops.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce a hard per-query CPU budget (e.g. 500ms wall-clock via context cancellation); cap nodes-visited at 200K and return best-known-path with a `partial=true` flag; isolate long-haul queries to a dedicated pool (separate deployment) via a request hint `mode=long_distance` so short-trip latency doesn't degrade; precompute transit tables between top-1000 metro-pair S2 cells so truly long routes become a table lookup + two short CH searches.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram `routing_nodes_visited` per query — alert on p99 > 50K; track `routing_inflight_requests` per pod and page at >400 (80% of cap); monitor `routing_query_duration_p99_ms` > 800ms sustained for 2 min.

bottlenecks.title: Live-traffic edge-weight updates contend with query threads on the shared graph
bottlenecks.trigger: CCH lets the traffic layer plug in live edge weights without full CH re-preprocess, but weight updates arrive continuously (every 1-2 min for major metros, ~millions of edges touched per update) and must be applied to the in-memory graph while 100-500 concurrent route queries read from it. Under RW-lock contention or copy-on-write page faults during update, query latency is dominated by lock waits not graph traversal.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic sawtooth in p95/p99 latency aligned with traffic-update cadence (spikes every 60-120s); CPU profiler shows threads blocked in futex/RWLock; rush-hour reroutes that should benefit from fresh traffic actually get worse because updates arrive mid-query and invalidate the customization table.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a double-buffered weight table (active + staging) with an atomic pointer swap — updates write to staging, single CAS flips readers to the new version, old buffer GC'd after inflight drains; shard weight updates by geographic region (S2 cell) so a Tokyo update doesn't block SF queries; batch updates to 5-10s cadence and apply deltas rather than full tables; pin weight-update thread to a dedicated core to avoid stealing CPU from query threads.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `routing_weight_update_duration_ms` and correlate with `routing_query_latency_p99` — alert when correlation coefficient > 0.6 over a 10-min window; monitor `routing_rwlock_wait_time_seconds` per pod and page on >50ms/sec sustained; dashboard per-minute p99 latency to spot periodic sawtooth patterns.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Routing Service is here For Google Maps, "directions from A to B" is a fundamentally different workload from tile serving or place search. It's not a lookup — it's a **graph search** over the world road network (~2B nodes, ~3B edges). You can't cache the answer because every origin/destination pair is unique and live traffic changes the edge weights every minute. So there has to be a dedicated service that holds the road graph in RAM and runs a shortest-path algorithm on every request. The key design choice is using **Contraction Hierarchies (CH)**, which preprocesses shortcut edges offline so that even a 1000 km query terminates in ~100ms instead of seconds. ## What happens without it If you tried to serve routing out of the same box as tiles or search, two things break. First, routing is CPU-heavy and latency-variable (50-300ms), so a burst of route requests would starve the tile path of threads — users would see pans stutter. Second, without CH preprocessing, each route would run plain Dijkstra across the global graph. An SF→LA query visiting tens of millions of nodes would take 2-5 seconds; users hit "Directions," stare at a spinner, and give up. ## The arithmetic Capacity says **10M route requests/day ≈ 115 QPS average, ~500 QPS peak**. With CH visiting only ~1284 nodes for a 616 km route (vs tens of millions for Dijkstra), one server can handle ~10 routes/sec on a single core. Plain Dijkstra would need 50× more CPU to hit the same SLO — economically unworkable. ## Trade-off CH preprocessing takes hours and ~80GB RAM per replica, but online queries become interactive.

steps.title: Routing service runs bidirectional CH search
steps.action: Converts origin/dest to nearest graph nodes, then runs a bidirectional Dijkstra on the augmented (CH shortcuts) graph.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Contraction Hierarchies bidirectional search (pseudocode)
origin_node = nearest_node(37.7749, -122.4194) # ~OSM way 12345
dest_node = nearest_node(34.0522, -118.2437) # ~OSM way 67890 fwd_q = MinHeap([(0, origin_node)])
bwd_q = MinHeap([(0, dest_node)])
fwd_dist, bwd_dist = {}, {}
best = float('inf') while fwd_q or bwd_q: # Forward step — only traverse upward in CH rank u, d = fwd_q.pop for v, w in upward_edges(u): nd = d + w_with_traffic(u, v) if nd < fwd_dist.get(v, INF): fwd_dist[v] = nd fwd_q.push((nd, v)) if v in bwd_dist: best = min(best, nd + bwd_dist[v]) # Symmetric backward step... # Terminate when top of both heaps > best path = unpack_shortcuts(meeting_node) # expand CH shortcuts to real road edges
return { distance_m: 616000, duration_s: 21600, geometry: encoded_polyline(path) }
steps.note: Only ~1284 nodes visited for a 616 km route — that's the magic of CH vs plain Dijkstra, which would visit tens of millions.

steps.action: Wraps the result with turn-by-turn instructions (generated by a separate post-processor) and returns JSON.
steps.codeOrCommand:

}

tradeoffs.chosen: Vector tiles (PBF) over pre-rendered raster PNGs
tradeoffs.rationale: Vector tiles are an order of magnitude smaller over the wire and let the client restyle (night mode, language swap) without re-fetching, at the cost of more CPU on the client GPU. Raster is simpler but blows up storage by a factor of ten per style.

tradeoffs.chosen: Contraction hierarchies plus bidirectional Dijkstra, not raw A*
tradeoffs.rationale: Raw Dijkstra on a continent-scale graph takes multiple seconds; A* with great-circle heuristic helps but still scans millions of nodes. Contraction hierarchies pre-compute shortcut edges so the online search touches tens of thousands of nodes in under 100 ms.

tradeoffs.chosen: Edge-weight deltas in Redis, not graph rebuilds
tradeoffs.rationale: Rebuilding the contraction hierarchy every few minutes would cost tens of CPU-hours. Overlaying a weight delta at query time costs a single hash lookup per relaxed edge and keeps traffic freshness under one minute.

tradeoffs.chosen: Custom trie for prefix speed, Elasticsearch for fuzzy matching
tradeoffs.rationale: A trie answers strict prefix queries in microseconds but cannot handle typos; Elasticsearch handles fuzz via edit distance but is slower. Splitting the two keeps the hot 80 percent of queries on the trie and the rest on ES.

tradeoffs.chosen: Immutable tiles keyed by render version, not mutable overwrite
tradeoffs.rationale: Mutable tiles would require per-tile cache invalidation across a global CDN, which is almost impossible to do cleanly. Immutable versioned URLs let a rollback flip a single style pointer and make every CDN cache entry correct.
